explanation: The default launch policy for `std::async`—used when no explicit policy is provided—is the bitwise OR of the two explicit policies: `std::launch::async | std::launch::deferred`. This allows the C++ implementation (e.g., the OS or runtime library) to decide whether to run the task on a new thread immediately (async) or defer it until `get()`/`wait()` is called (deferred). This flexibility means the developer cannot rely on the task running asynchronously without explicitly specifying the `async` policy.
code_example:
auto fut1 = std::async(func); // Default policy
auto fut2 = std::async(std::launch::async | std::launch::deferred, func); // Equivalent to default
practical_example: A developer uses default `std::async` hoping for concurrent execution, but on a resource-constrained system, the runtime chooses the `deferred` policy, leading to unexpected sequential execution and performance bottlenecks when the results are queried.
chapter: Item 35: Prefer task-based programming to thread-based programming
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
